subject: WSJ Travel: Chasing Airline Status 🎩
body_text:
96 Plus, Hyatt changes and holiday travel tips   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser             Sponsored by       Dawn Gilbertson   Help Our Travel Columnist Chase Airline Status (Or Talk Her Out of It)   Plus, Hyatt changes and holiday travel tips   Happy Friday! Hope your flights go smoothly if you’re getting away early for Thanksgiving. Just think of me on Thanksgiving Eve when I’ll be in row 27 on a cross-country red eye to Hartford. 

   I don’t need to sum up the big travel news because so many of us lived it: the aftermath of the groundstop. My colleagues Andrew Tangel and Drew FitzGerald had a scoop on the router that started it all. Airlines reporter Aly Sider went behind-the-scenes at Southwest , which took pains to avoid a repeat of its holiday meltdown in 2022. On the personal front, my mom made it home after being stranded in Baltimore . There are lessons in that column for future meltdowns, namely snag a hotel ASAP. Among the few winners, it seems: airport bartenders . 

   In other news, semiprivate carrier JSX announced plans to fly between New York and Dallas beginning in February. Hyatt unveiled loyalty program changes and details of its new partnership with Delta. And Grand Canyon National Park hotels reopened after severe flooding in August led to water restrictions that closed hotels like El Tovar. 

   Before we dive into this week’s main thing, I’ll leave you with a couple of holiday travel tips. #1: If you have a passport and TSA PreCheck and haven’t opted into TSA PreCheck Touchless ID with your airline, stop everything you’re doing and sign up now. Thank me when you breeze through the security line. #2: Pick up your relatives at the airport this holiday season. The goodwill and warm fuzzies are priceless. (You get a pass in certain cities like New York, but even then could meet them and ride public transportation together.) 

       Airline status chase     PATRICK T. FALLON/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES   To chase airline status or not?

   That’s the question facing many frequent fliers as year-end approaches. Airlines, gunning for last-minute bookings or credit-card spending, keep reminding us how close we are to that next tier in their loyalty programs.

   I can’t be loyal to a single airline in this job because I write about ‘em all. The only airline I routinely have status on is Southwest. But I’ve taken 59 flights this year and am tantalizingly close to (mostly minor) status on several airlines for the first time.

   The perks like free bags, seat assignments and priority boarding are nice in this era of sky-high fees and the ever-present fight for bin space. (Potential upgrades aren’t really a consideration unless you have top-tier status.)

   You can get some of the status perks with an airline credit card, of course. But I only have American and Southwest cards.

   So here’s the question: Should I go for it? If so, on which airlines and how?

   AI has plenty of ideas, and I’ve got some, too, but I want to hear your ideas. If you’re a frequent flier or points-and-miles geek doing the same math, no matter the status level, let me know how you’re approaching it or if you’ve given up and will be a free agent in 2027.

   My editors have given me a budget of up to $1,000 for this status challenge. Tell me how to best spend it (or not) for the biggest payoff in 2027. I want to do it through traveling, not random credit-card spending, and as efficiently as possible. AI told me to get a bunch of subscriptions I don’t need to rack up American points. No thanks.

   Here’s where I stand, from smallest gap to close to biggest. My home airport is Phoenix. I likely have at least two more work trips this year.

   • Southwest Airlines: I’m three one-way flights away from retaining my A List status for 2027, when it will be called silver status under major program changes announced in October. This is the easiest get, but with high fares even on short hops, three one-way flights could eat up a lot of money. 

   • American Airlines : I have temporary platinum status through Dec. 16 thanks to a corporate status match in August. I’ve come to like the perks even if I’ve never been upgraded and live in an AA hub. My shortage: 5,608 points to reach the 25,000 requirement to keep Platinum. I’ve already unlocked Gold for 2027 but would really like to close this gap. The betting money seems to be on finding a hotel offering a bounty of points but I’m open!

   • Delta: I’m $430 (medallion qualifying dollars, that is) away from the $5,000 spend required to hit silver status. I’ve had silver before and it’s nothing special, but you do get the aforementioned free bag and slightly better boarding and seat assignments. Plus, I’m so close.

   • United : I’m 2,521 (premier qualifying) points short of silver. This one’s probably out of reach and not worth it. Agree? 

   • Alaska : I’m more than two-thirds of the way to silver status but still need 6,471 points to hit it. 

   • JetBlue: I’ve already locked in Mosaic 1 for next year thanks to a business-class flight to London earlier this year. I’d need 58 tiles to hit level 2 so that’s a nonstarter. 

   Suggest away! I’ll report back in a column later this year.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here .

   • You’re probably using AI chatbots all wrong as you plan that next trip. Here’s the secret to getting better recommendations . 

   • If the meltdown gave you fits, save these tips for the next one.

   • Gotta go next time you visit New York? Check out the city’s new high-tech loos .

She recently returned from Paris and picked up souvenirs. Not at the airport or a touristy stand by the Eiffel Tower, but at a grocery store and pharmacy. She bought dark chocolate and Champagne at Monoprix for under $50 and loaded up on lip balms, face masks and other goodies at a French pharmacy. Try it on your next trip.

       Travel Math 🧮   85.9%   The occupancy rate at U.S. airport hotels last Friday during the groundstop, according to CoStar. A year ago, it was 70.3%. Room rates rose, too, of course. The average daily rate was $150.03, a 13.3% increase.

       And We Quote 💬   “It was a giant pain in the rear but we never felt destabilized. We always felt like things were between the guardrails. It was just a lot of work. It was an awful lot of work to get through.”

   — Southwest Airlines Chief Operating Officer Andrew Watterson, on the airline’s battle plan during the groundstop.

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on our tips for handling an airline meltdown : 

   • “They need to know to call their travel agent. Oh, most don’t have one! They thought they could do it all by themselves and save some money. They don’t understand the value of a professional travel agent. I’ve had the same travel agent for more than 30 years. She is relentless and could rip the throat out of a lion. In over 4 million miles, I have never slept in an airport. She always answers her phone on holidays, evenings, Saturdays and Sundays.” — Mark Dennen, Massachusetts 

   …on trans-Atlantic cruises : 

   • “Just sending you a short thank-you note. Last November, my partner and I read your column on a trans-Atlantic cruise from Rome and were inspired to book one. We returned this past Friday (luckily, two hours before the nationwide ground stop) from a 13-day trans-Atlantic repositioning cruise on Royal Caribbean’s Explorer of the Seas (from Barcelona, with stops in Cartagena, Majorca, the Azores and Bermuda). Your column was great preparation for what to expect, as this experience was different from other cruises we’ve taken before. We’re huge fans of your column and look forward to more helpful travel recommendations and future inspirations from you.” — Howard Suskin, Illinois 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       Travel-arious 🤣   Influencer Morgan Evelyn Cook, a contestant on “The Traitors: New Blood” this season, came up with a list of “inconvenient but funny” requests for the next wave of tech outages across different businesses.

   If airlines are a target again, she wants the people responsible to change the carry-on rules so fanny packs don’t count toward the two-item limit.

   “A fanny pack takes up literally no space,” she said in an Instagram Reel . “We all know that as soon as we’re on the plane the fanny pack is coming out of the bag that it was just stuffed into. So it’s like, ‘Why are we doing this?’”

       Cheers and Jeers 🤷   I could fill this newsletter with cheers and jeers after being on the road for 3 ½ weeks.

   Cheers to American Airlines’ new snack lineup in economy. I’m not a Biscoff fan (heresy, I know) and loved to see the Tiny Tate’s Bake Shop chocolate chip cookies on my flight out of Miami last Friday.

   Jeers to the continuing mess that is Europe’s new entry/exit system. It gummed up our cruise ship boarding out of Rome in late October. Despite having been fingerprinted a few times on earlier trips , the kiosk still sent me to the manual passport-check line.

   Big (continued) jeers to airline bag fees. I paid $100 for my mom to check two bags one way on Southwest Airlines. Those costs add up for a family.

       One Final Shot 📷     DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   I caught this sunset in the North Atlantic Ocean on a trans-Atlantic crossing on Celebrity Cruises earlier this month.
